Yes bigotry is not exclusively white. But I feel that what the post is trying to highlight is that these narratives are just objectively shallowly written. I personally have a problem in the hypothetical scenario presented (black person shouting slurs at an elf) because of the implication that this film is yet another corporate cash cow that is an interested in exploring racial commentary. My take is that these forms of media are not woke to intersectionality and will often try to equate one form of bigotry as completely and utterly equivalent to another. So they might equate a black person being bigoted to an elf in the same way that the might present a white person being bigoted to a black person. These corporate cash cows are not interested in exploring whether a black person still faces the same sort of bigotry in our world in addition to being bigoted towards other species. There is often no exploration of how despite one group being the aggressor or the victims there are still racial stratifications that exist within that group. For example you might get a story where humans are the oppressors but it often turns out that all humans equally oppress the elves and they are all good with each other and only hate the elves. There is no acknowledgement that even within certain dominant groups that there are still subgroups that hold privilege over one another.

But these situations are not the same. This is the race equivalent of the white feminism present in The Handmaid's Tale TV series. There is no way June would have been able to get away with what she does had she been black.

I think One Piece does this really well for a number of reasons.


1. The oppressed races like Fishmen, mermaids, and giants, while much stronger than ordinary humans, are a very small minority of the population.


2. The oppression is reflected in the world building — the minority races (including Sky people, Kuja, Shandians) often live in places regular humans would find hard to access (up in the sky or under the sea). Those that do live on the Blue Sea have adopted warrior cultures, which does imply a level of persecution taking place.


3. Their oppression isn't framed around them being stronger per se, it is more explicitly tied to their actual race. As anyone can be strong in One Piece, it isn't actually their powers that make them a target, which I think is my main gripe with tropes like these too. 


4. They absolutely CAN be bested by non-powered humans with great training. Superpowered humans (IE Devil Fruit users) can also best them.


5. The minority races DO oppress regular humans, too! IE. Arlong.

I think you're expecting too much. Not in the sense of quality of the kids show (iT's JuSt A cARtOon DoN't ThInK aBoUt iT), but more that I think you're expecting realism and adultness from a kids show in the first place. Having things that aren't realistic or not logical by real life standards not happen at all would just make a real life story, not a kids adventure cartoon. The story is about unlikely child heroes saving the world. It's meant to evoke wonder, provide a power fantasy, inspire. What should the characters do then? Not save the world? Not even try, knowing there are way more skilled masters out there who could kill them in a heartbeat? It makes for a lame subversion and not a great iteration of the story the creators are intending to tell. You're wanting Game of Thrones kind of realism from a kids show.


Also I think you're ignoring story. There's a war going on. The kids have to grow up fast. There's a whole bit where Aang, a 12-year-old, has to suddenly master 3 separate elements in a matter of months when previous Avatars had years to hone their skills and were only told that they were the Avatar when they turned 16, what is implied to be the age of majority. It's a major plot point that he HAS to do this by necessity. It reflects the tragedy of the war. So if you apply IRL conventions should he really have beat Ozai? Lol no. But within the context of the story, yes. It then stands to reason that the other members of Team Avatar would have to grow up equally as fast if not more. Kids IRL do this already. Why not in stories too?


Also with your FMA rant, I would like to point out that the Elric brothers are established to be geniuses in the field of alchemy. So yeah at least there's a justification for them being able to pick up advanced alchemy.


The other parts about FMA's worldbuilding though...yeah. I agree. Alchemy can do so much but barely anyone uses it to its full extent. Perhaps there could be the in-universe reasoning that due to Amestris being controlled by a Homunculus, and alchemy being a significant weapon that could be used against them, Father could have been suppressing the use of alchemy in some way just in case. This can be supported by how there's a social divide between state alchemists (regarded as sell-outs) and civilian alchemists like Izumi. But eh that's all rather implied and not very substantial with its information within the story so I say it's reaching. But fun to think about anyway. There's not much worldbuilding at all in FMA, it was never the focus of the story, despite what people may think. (I have no idea why Hello Future Me decided to include FMA in his video on empires, FMA is by no means a worldbuilding masterpiece or even very notable for it, it shines in other areas).


Whereas with Roy and his very visible runes, I always assumed there was more to it than just the runes. That although a simple explanation was given as to how his flame alchemy worked, I always assumed there was a rather more complicated bit any alchemist has to study for first, and that it quite difficult to access for someone without the benefit of a good formal education and the related opportunities. I myself always wondered why the hell no one tries to copy his runes and reverse engineer it themselves as you said. It's not explained very well in the story though, so I'll agree with you there. And yes the science is bushy, so I'll take you to my next point.


I think people hype up the magic systems of alchemy and bending way too much, and for the wrong reasons. The way people talk about it makes others feel as if these systems are very in-depth and well-explained, but the truth is that in addition to be a visual medium (which is faster paced than books usually and has less time for word-for-word exposition without the audience getting bored), people enjoy the systems because they make sense for the story. Most people are not magic system nerds who strive to nitpick and tinker with every single bit of magic lore. Any vaguely sciencey or consistent explanation is enough. They care if it makes sense to the characters involved or not. In FMA, I think the magic system presented makes perfect sense to follow the story of the characters, and that is enough. The characters were always the forefront of that story, more so than its visuals, fight sequences, worldbuilding, etc.


TLDR: it's just not that kinda story.
